title: Porodica Mrvice
reviewerNotes: Full draft to Lesson 1 exemplar bar. Ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Mrvica adopts Ana. Amira’s café regulars start to feel like family.

vocabulary: Name majka, otac, sestra, brat, baba, djed, sin, and kći
Use porodica, prijatelj, prijateljica, and mačka around the café
Use the possessives moj, moja, tvoj, and tvoja

Mrvica as the café’s unofficial boss

grammar.title: Gender intro. He or she words
grammar.explanation: Many Bosnian nouns feel masculine or feminine. A quick beginner tip helps. Words ending in -a are often feminine, such as majka, sestra, mačka, and porodica. Short words without that ending are often masculine in this lesson, such as otac, brat, and djed.

grammar.title: Moj / moja and tvoj / tvoja
grammar.explanation: Moj means my before a masculine noun. Moja means my before a feminine noun. The same split holds for informal your with tvoj and tvoja. Say Moj brat and Moja sestra. Do not mix them yet.

grammar.title: Who is who. On je / Ona je
grammar.explanation: Reuse biti from Lesson 2 to point and name people. Say On je moj prijatelj. Say Ona je moja prijateljica. Say Ona je Mrvica, mačka! The same short pattern works for one bossy cat too.

culture.title: Café family and one small boss
culture.body: In Sarajevo, a good café can feel like a living room. Regulars greet the owner by name, share news, and claim “their” chair. Amira’s place works the same way. Ana, Emir, and the usual guests start to feel like porodica. Family you choose. Mrvica the cat patrols the tables, steals warmth, and somehow adopts Ana. Learn the family words, then use them for blood relatives and for the people (and cats) who make a city feel like home.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. Family words + gender
lessonBlocks.body: Build the family tree with majka, otac, sestra, brat, baba, djed, sin, and kći. Say each word aloud twice. Mark the -a words as feminine in your notes. Add porodica for family and mačka for cat. Ana draws a tiny family tree in her notebook, then draws Mrvica at the top. Emir laughs and says To je porodica Mrvice!
tips: For this lesson’s nouns, -a endings are often feminine.
Kći needs ć. Include the special letter.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. Moj / moja at Amira’s
lessonBlocks.body: Claim people with possessives. Say Moj prijatelj Emir. Say Moja prijateljica Amira. Ask Moja mačka? Mrvica decides that Ana is hers. Practice the pairs Moj otac and Moja majka, then Tvoj brat and Tvoja sestra. Walk the café and point. Say Ona je Amira. Say On je Emir. Say Ona je Mrvica. The win in this lesson is short true sentences rather than a full case chart.
tips: Keep Moj, Moja, On je, and Ona je ready.
Match moj or moja to the noun’s gender.

funFacts.title: Baba and djed
funFacts.body: Baba and djed are everyday words for grandmother and grandfather. Families may use affectionate variants, but these two open many stories. Learners meet them early because family talk starts with the oldest generation. Learn baba and djed first, then build the rest of the family tree around them.

funFacts.title: Prijatelj vs prijateljica
funFacts.body: Bosnian marks the gender of friend with two clear forms. Prijatelj is masculine, and prijateljica is feminine. Ana calls Emir prijatelj and Amira prijateljica for that reason. Get the pair right early, because real friendships need the right word from day one.

funFacts.title: Mrvica means little crumb
funFacts.body: Mrvica means little crumb, and the café cat lives up to it. She believes every lap and every lokum crumb is hers. Family vocabulary in this lesson somehow includes one very pushy mačka. If she claims Ana, Emir will treat that adoption as official.

funFacts.title: Chosen family at the table
funFacts.body: Calling café regulars porodica is half joke and half truth. People share news, chairs, and kahva until the table feels like home. Warmth is part of the language lesson, not an extra decoration. When Ana uses family words at Amira’s, she is naming both blood relatives and chosen company.

civicContext.title: Three presidents share one top office
civicContext.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina’s top executive is split along ethnic lines deliberately. The Presidency has three members, one Bosniak, one Croat, and one Serb, under the Dayton settlement that ended the war. That shared office is meant to keep each constituent people represented at the highest level of the state. Family talk at a café table therefore happens in a country where even the top job is a three-person arrangement, not a single national president.
